healthInfo.healthcareSystem: Mixed public-private system (IMSS for residents, ISSSTE for public employees). Tourists access private healthcare.
healthInfo.qualityNotes: Private healthcare in major cities (Mexico City, Cancun, Puerto Vallarta) is good and affordable by US standards. Public hospitals can be overcrowded. Ensure you are treated at a reputable private facility. Medical tourism is popular for dental work and cosmetic surgery.
healthInfo.pharmacyHours: Many pharmacies open 24/7, especially in tourist areas. Chain pharmacies like Farmacias Guadalajara, Benavides, and CVS are widely available.
healthInfo.pharmacyTips: Many medications that require prescriptions in the US are available OTC in Mexico, including antibiotics. However, it's still best to have a prescription. Keep medications in original packaging. Watch for counterfeit medications — buy from reputable chains.
healthInfo.prescriptionRules: Foreign prescriptions are generally not accepted for controlled substances. You may need a local Mexican prescription from a doctor. Report all medications to customs at entry.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is a controlled substance. A Mexican prescription may be required.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A medical prescription and declaration may be required. Check with Mexican consulate before travel.

restrictedMeds.name: Opioid pain medications (morphine, oxycodone, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring a prescription and customs declaration.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis/THC products
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis remains illegal for tourists despite decriminalization for personal use by Mexican residents.

healthInfo.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English or Spanish listing all medications with generic names. Bring all prescription medications in original containers. Declare all medications at Mexican customs. Carry your doctor's prescription, translated into Spanish if possible.

travelInsurance.tips: Purchase travel insurance that covers medical emergencies, hospitalization, and medical evacuation. Mexico's private hospitals expect payment upfront or guarantees from your insurance. Ensure your policy has a 24/7 assistance line in English.

recommended: Typhoid (for extended travel or rural areas)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for most travelers. Yellow fever vaccine may be required if arriving from an endemic area.

healthInfo.waterNotes: Do not drink tap water. Drink bottled water only. In resorts and major cities, ice and water from filtered machines is generally safe. Use bottled water for brushing teeth.
healthInfo.foodSafetyTips: In tourist areas and reputable restaurants, food safety is generally good. Be cautious with street food in rural areas. Avoid raw salads in areas with poor water quality. Seafood should be freshly cooked. Watch out for traveler's diarrhea — treat with ORS and seek medical care if severe.
healthInfo.medicalTourismNote: Mexico is a major medical tourism destination, especially for dental work, cosmetic surgery, and weight loss procedures. Costs are 50-70% lower than in the US.
